utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis with Belinda Pidwell and our case manager, Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I hand the hard copy to the witness, Your Honour, of the document we were looking at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Witness. I would remind you that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. When we left off yesterday we had been talking about some notes from your diary concerning your interviews with some of the Yellow Wasps that were arrested in Zvornik in late July 1992. And I've had the usher hand you the hard copy. I think we're on page 3 of the English and page 4 in the B/C/S in e-court. It's page 3 for you, Witness. We were talking about item number 6, the list for liquidation of unwanted Serbs. And then you had told me about -- that you had not seen such a list but you had seen the list with some names of some 6- or 700 Muslims or Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the end of the day yesterday I think you were telling us about the time when you were briefly with or a member of the VRS military police and you went to Celopek Dom to take a look at persons detained there to see if you knew anyone from your time working before the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I apologise. I would indicate that we've been looking at 65 ter 1439, 1439. Now, on this page 3, item number 7 it talks about Zuco's stay in Pale and he was there twice. Do you recall where you got that information that Zuco had been to Pale twice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From him during our informative talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you also personally interview his brother, Dusan, known as Repic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'd like to show you 65 ter 3020. This will come up on the screen in a moment, sir. Do you recognise that document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The writing style is familiar, but I would like to be able to read to the end to see if it is me or one of my colleagues. But since I was the one who conducted the interview, perhaps it's possible that somebody else actually drafted the statement. I cannot see the end of the document. I cannot see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, it appears that the only signature we have on this statement is that of Mr. Vuckovic, the person giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that typical of the way these kind of statements were taken in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't typical. The usual thing was that the person who was conducting the interview would put their signature and the person also who was giving the statement would sign, the date would be entered, and also the initials or the signature of the typist who was typing it out. I've never taken a statement like this or permitted the person who was interviewed to sign it like this. The letters are a little bit small, so I find it hard to see. But I would not submit a statement like this to anyone. I don't know who took this statement, maybe somebody else, the people from the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But your standard practice was always to sign the statement along with the witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see that in a whole series of cases, including the Yellow Wasps case. You could see how I took statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that just your personal practice, or was that a requirement under the rules in the MUP, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the basis of MUP, rules, and rules had to be respected. As to why somebody took a statement like this, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said earlier that you thought this might possibly have been taken by someone on the state security side of the house. Do you know what the rules were regarding how they took statements? Because of the nature of their work, did the operatives who took statements not sign, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I didn't work in that service so I don't know their rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could turn back again to 1439. Again, Witness, this is the hard copy document that you have in front of you. These notes from your diary, were they taken contemporaneously with the events that you're describing; that is, did you write these notes at the time you were conducting the interviews of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the time-period, yes. This was the first diary that I received as an operative in the ministry of Republika Srpska. I received an old diary. I didn't have anything else and that's when I began.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I want to go to page 16 in the English, that's page 16 for you in the hard copy, sir. And then B/C/S in e-court would be page 17. We see there a reference to a meeting on the 15th of August, 1992. Is that a meeting you attended; and if so, what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the members of the group. Probably that was asked by my boss, Goran Macar, and the cabinet to go into the field and to see what the situation was as far as crime was among the police forces and all other problems that dated from April up until July/August, in that area. I was accompanied by Nikola Milanovic and the police administration was represented I think by Cedomir Tosic or Radenko Vujicic. I'm not sure which one, and I think there was one more operative Milomir Orasanin. These are all old experienced operatives who had more than 20 or 25 years of service at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again intervention in the transcript, page 5, line 3, he said -- he was giving specifically which cabinet he meant. I don't see that in transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, it appears that the translation didn't pick up which cabinet you were going to the office for. Did you name that; and if so, could you repeat it for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hierarchy in the MUP begins from the minister. When I say the "cabinet," I imply -- I mean the minister. That is where all the ideas flow down towards the administration. It can be the police administration, the crime investigations administration, or some other one. The minister would see the problem at collegium meetings with the chief of the centres when he had an overview of the problems, then I assume that he would send a dispatch to the police administrations or the crime investigations administrations or the chiefs of those administrations, and they in turn would pick the people who would go out into the field, review the situation, and make a complete report, and then report back to him. That is how it worked, and then you would have other matters and meetings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the next page for you, sir, page 17 in e-court of the English and 18 of the B/C/S, it appears to be further notes about this meeting on the 15th of August. And you note that about 20 operatives are present. Could you explain for me and the Judges, what is an operative in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a kind of name that is used frequently for a person that has special police authority. It could be a uniformed officer or a civilian officer. We simply refer to such persons as operatives. We don't say a police inspector or a crime investigation inspector; we would just refer to them as operatives, short.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how is that different from just a regular policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference would be, for example, first of all in the degree of education; then the security and the difficulty of the assignments, compared to just regular policemen and regular crimes. I'm not underestimating any single policeman in Republika Srpska or anywhere else who worked as beat officers and didn't finish university. This is something else. But in order to be an operative in the crime-fighting unit or the police unit, there was some conditions, preconditions, and that would be the education completed, work experience, and some other factors. And if you permit me, I can say that our minister was one of the best students in the school for internal affairs and started off as a regular policeman and then became a minister. Mr. Zupljanin also was a very good operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've seen the term in some MUP documents, the term which is translated as "authorised official of the MUP." Can you explain to me what that is and how it differs from "operative."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: MUP is an abbreviation for "Ministarstvo Unutrasnjih Poslova," Ministry of Internal Affairs. So we say -- instead of a security services centre or a public security station or a police station, we just refer to them as "MUP." That is a common term. There is I think also a title and I referred to it yesterday. What the Ministry of Internal Affairs is and how it was structured, what its administrations are, what the security centres are, how they were formed according to the departments at a lower level, and then I also talked about the public security station and its department, how that was formed, and that is the lowest organisational unit. All together, though, we referred to all those offices as the MUP; that was a common name. It doesn't mean -- if somebody says that they are an employee of the security station or if they are an operative, that they made a mistake by saying that they were in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I may have confused you with my question. I was interested primarily in the definition of "authorised official." I take it that not all employees of the MUP were authorised officials. For example, the janitor may not have been an authorised official. Can you explain to us what an authorised official was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An authorised official is a person that has an official identification card and has a special authority. This is not something that everyone had. There are other MUP services in the centres and the stations. These are legal departments, analysis departments, and persons who worked there were not authorised officials. So official ID cards were issued only to policemen who were beat policemen, who worked on public law and order, to operatives or to crime-fighting police officers, and then going up towards the top of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. So these were people who dealt with crimes, the work of the police. There was a war going on. People had to be taken to the lines. They had this authority and this is where the difference lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And connected with holding the position of an authorised official, were there certain privileges that attached? For example, were authorised officials allowed to carry weapons, to make arrests? Can you give me some examples?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authorised officials had the description of what they were permitted to do in their personal ID card. They were allowed to carry weapons, they were allowed to enter somebody's apartment or official office, they could confiscate a vehicle in case of an emergency. All these things were strictly described and entered in the professional ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it then that all operatives were authorised officials; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On this page, at the bottom of the page, there is a point I think at the very bottom of the page in my English translation says: "Monitoring of genocide and war crimes against the Serbian people, in accordance with the UZSK dispatch." First of all, can you tell me what UZSK stands for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an abbreviation in 1992 which meant "Uprava Za Suzbijanje Kriminaliteta" crime-fighting administration, and this title was in use for a year or a year and a half, and it was changed to the UKP, "Uprava Krim Policije," crime police administration. So this is an old title from the communist times, the UZSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said that all operatives are authorised officials, but is it correct that not all authorised officials were operatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot understand that, that somebody who's authorised to carry a weapon can enter somebody else's apartment or other areas for a search or to detain somebody as stated in their official identification card for them not to be an operative. I cannot understand that. For me, that is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's the same thing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that was a question I had thought about asking, but that answer is not what I thought would have been given. I'm a little confused, then, Witness, by your earlier answer. I sort of understood "operatives" to be people like yourself who I guess the nearest analogy in my experience in America would be a detective, somebody who wears plain clothes and interviews suspects and investigates crimes, versus the regular policemen, the beat policemen who drives in a patrol car, walks a foot patrol and wears a uniform, and -- is there a distinction between the two, or would you call the regular policeman wearing the standard uniform and doing a beat patrol an operative as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct, yes. It does seem to be like that. But amongst ourselves, when we use the term that somebody's an operative, I think that that didn't get in the way of inspectors doing their job in relation to crime in relation to a beat policeman in a certain sector who had to know who was living in that area, what is the structure of the population, how many people had criminal files, how many crimes were being committed in that area. We referred to them as operatives too. A policeman had to do a certain amount of work in the previous system, and then in the system after the war, that can actually quite come close to the amount of work to an operative who had to work in a specific field, for example, homicide or thefts or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move back then to page 17 of your notes. This dispatch about monitoring genocide and war crimes against the Serbian people, by whom had that been sent if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it came from the minister's office through our first chief who received it, read it, designated people who would go out into the field and convey what was contained in the dispatch. I personally did not read it at the time, but I heard about it at the meeting chaired by Mr. Nikola Milanovic, a long-time operative, and that meeting was held with the representatives of politic -- police -- public -- police stations in that area, the Doboj region. It was related to the deaths among Serbs and Bosniaks. However, when an operative who worked in the Doboj centre, he was a seasoned operative, reported that from April to June - that's before the corridor - they had 11 or 13 murders of Bosniaks in town and criminal complaints were filed, he was told, "Don't brief us on that now. We'll discuss it later. Why didn't you send it to the prosecutor's office? Let's see what we are going to do next."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me have you turn to page 19 in your hard copy, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 19 of the English and 20 of the B/C/S in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the top of the page the first point in my English translation says: "Number of operative posts filled in the Doboj centre. It is the intention of the ministry to select and hire staff." Do you recall what that was about? Who in the ministry was going to select and hire staff for what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war began, let's say in early May 1992 as far as the Doboj region is concerned, around -- many people were admitted into the reserve force of the public security station Doboj and CSB Doboj, and they were not properly vetted as to whether they had any record or whether they were quite fit. And in order to clean the ranks a bit, it was decided that we had to let such people go. And the public security stations as well as the CSB knew well who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that mean that the new employees were going to be picked at the ministry level as opposed to being picked in Doboj at the CSB or some lower level, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way they were admitted into the public security station of Doboj and the CSB of Doboj, I suppose, they did not have the ministry's approval. I mean, I can only suppose because I know that Milosevic [as interpreted] was chief and he had a deputy who is now mayor. They did not have any communication practically, although they were working in the same house. And Dusan Zivkovic was not speaking to Andrija and Andrija was not speaking to the chief. They admitted people on to the force any which way, the police or the crime investigation department. And there were some ridiculous applications that in my practice I came across. If the Trial Chamber wants to know, I can tell them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple questions there. At page 12, line 7, you say: "I know that" -- and it's been translated as: " ... I know that Milosevic was chief and he had a deputy who is now mayor." I think that name was not heard properly. Who was the chief, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the name. He's a local, but if it comes to me I'll tell you. But everyone knows who I'm talking about. He's a member of the SDS, and it was through SDS channels that he came to that position, just like Andrija Bjelosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. I think I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis, I believe the witness didn't understand your question at all because he just mentioned the proper name of the chief of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to get from you, Witness, was the name of the chief of the CSB, and if you can just confirm for us, it was Andrija Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andrija Bjelosevic. He resided in Derventa, worked in the defence ministry. He had some sort of university degree in political science or some humanitarian degree, and through the party he came to be chief of the centre in May 1992, a very bad police officer, no professional training, did not exercise his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to page 19 in your hard copy -- I'm sorry, page 20 in your hard copy, page 20 of the English, page 21 of the B/C/S in e-court. I've got questions about the last two entries on this page, Witness, and the first of those in English is translated as: "Appeal to authorised officials not to engage in any kind of shady deals." Do you recall what that was about when you wrote that down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the topics at the meeting. In the ministry by that time we had a large number of both anonymous and signed notes from the citizenry and workers of the Doboj centre that some officers abused their authority when entering the apartments of both Serb and non-Serb population. They would give -- they would sign protocols with false names and take away -- seize whatever they pleased. They would also illegally remove non-Serbs and drive them across the border towards Yugoslavia, the police check-points checked that. Such people were stigmatised, and they were sent to the front lines for stints up to one year. That was some sort of punishment. There were also other forms of abuse of authority, such as in detaining people, especially in Doboj. Those authorities had been in place in Doboj since before the war. Doboj was not destroyed as a town. It had all the institutions of authority, the prosecutor's office, the justice system, courts, prison. If the war had not happened, they could have gone on working lawfully. But what happened? The prison warden, an acquaintance of mine, Mirko, left that position of police -- of prison warden for reasons that only he knows. But probably because unlawful things were being done there, illegal arrests, illegal detention, people were being beaten and probably even killed in prison. Who ran the prison at the time I don't know, but I think it's easy to investigate, especially using the statement of the first justice minister, Momcilo Mandic. He could answer the question who was doing these things at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a question then about the next entry on this page at the very bottom. My English says: "Persons in the camps not to be taken out and no decisions to be made on their killing." What was that about when you wrote that note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the position taken by our office, that is, by our minister, the collegium as well, namely, that the police has no business with anything like camps or prisons. That was taken over by the Army of Republika Srpska. Whether it was a decision of the government or the then-War Presidency, I'm not sure. But around the 9th or 10th June, 1992, the decision came into force that all camps and prisons are now to be under the control of the corps and the police had no access there. If any individual policeman wilfully gained access and did something there, he would be held answerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The way that reads, it sounds to me as though this is something that had happened prior to 15 August, and that's why it's being discussed. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Let's take, for example, Samac. That case has been finalised, and I believe you have enough information about that. I would not like to go through it again but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I can stop you there. I don't think that's necessary right now. We'll have some more discussion about Samac later. If I could continue on in this document to page 25 in your hard copy, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 25 of the English, 26 B/C/S in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The second point in my English copy says: "Everybody was bringing people in and detaining them. It was arranged with the army that they would deal with the conscripts." Do you recall what that was about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there was a period in 1992 when it was agreed that if a military conscript is caught red-handed, he would be handled by the military police rather than the civilian police, in order not to confuse jurisdictions. Because there were examples in Modric and Derventa where guns were pulled between military policemen and civilian policemen over such disputes, and to avoid such things an agreement was made at the top, and I believe this is why this issue was raised at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 29 in your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And e-court 29 English, 30 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, the last or next-to-last entry, can you read that to me because in English the first word or so is -- not been able to be translated because it was found to be illegible. Can you read that whole entry for me? Something about employees taking Muslims from the city.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I wrote it, it reads: "It happens that this staff drives Muslims out of town and kills them ." Somebody at the meeting must have told us this. No specific murder was mentioned, but it was underlined as a recurring phenomenon so that we in the first and the second administration should know that such things were happening in the area of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where you've written "this staff" or as was translated in my English "these employees," who does that refer to, or what organ does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It referred to the police, police inspectors, men who worked in the security service, not necessarily authorised officers. I'll give you an example. Veljko Sulaja was chief of the general section for crime fighting, and he took one -- he took some of his close relatives, some of his in-laws, two or three Bosniaks up to Raca where the police stopped them. Mainly the Serbian police did not allow them entry. This case was recorded, dispatch was sent to Doboj. The State Security Service got involved, and he was suspended for six months and sent to the Army of Republika Srpska. I have other examples from Bijeljina. People attempted to take their relatives to safety, which is quite a normal thing to me. It's normal to help your own family. However, the police had prescribed certain rules and anyone who broke them had to suffer for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try and break this down so I understand clearly. I understand you to be saying that there were some instances where police and perhaps other Serbs, non-police, took Muslims out of town, perhaps across a border to some safety. Correct so far?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. There were cases of abuse where --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- these things were done for money.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my next question. In some cases it was done to help a relative or out of a good motive, sometimes for money, but in your statement you said some of these -- the staff or these employees were taking Muslims out of town and killing them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the lower part of this document. I believe it was Cvijo Anicic who briefed us on this. He was chief of general crime in Derventa. I noted down that sentence from him. Cvijo Anicic works currently as a judge at the lower court in Modrica. He's a serious manner, and while he worked in the police he was a good officer, as he's a good judge now. He said at that meeting that this was happening, but he did not explain any details to me or the wider audience. He probably had in mind some specific examples. Whether he shared this with Nikola or not, I could not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You said earlier that some of the Serbs who had been caught doing this, trying to take Muslims out were disciplined, sometimes removed from the police service and sent to the army and sent to the front lines; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any information about what happened to any police employees who took Muslims out and killed them? Were they removed from the service or punished or sent to the front lines, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be hard for me to give an answer to that question, I mean, if any of the policemen or operatives had committed such a crime, a war crime, that it became known and that they would be prosecuted for it…I cannot recall any such example, but I suppose there were such cases and that investigations against all individuals are on-going. As long as a person is still alive, I guess the time will come when they will be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1 I have a problem with the transcript. This is not what the witness said. 2 I don't know, maybe it's easier that I file the verification request, Your 3 Honours, in order to clarify the situation because the appropriate organs 4 can hear the tape and then make the necessary corrections. This is obviously 5 very important issue, and I'm reluctant to get up all the time and use up the 6 time and distract my friend, but I need to raise this issue. So whatever is 7 the instruction of the Trial Chamber. We can file the verification request. 8 [Trial Chamber confers] JUDGE HARHOFF: Mr. Zecevic, thanks for drawing 9 our attention to this. We've discussed it, and we're not quite sure of how 10 to best address this problem because judging from the number of interventions 11 that you've had this morning on this subject, it seems to be a recurrent 12 problem. And I don't know if there is any difficulty with interpreting 13 this witness's testimony into English, but the simple thing is always 14 to try and deal with it here, right on the spot, and that is to say to have 15 the witness repeat what he has just said in order to get the right meaning 16 out of it. But if it is a consistent issue, then we have to go the hard way 17 and you have to file then a request for verification and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honours, basically this is the first time in weeks that we are having this situation. Sometimes it is -- a part is missing, but this is a completely different issue. Now, in this case I believe the witness said quite differently from what is entered into the transcript. In my opinion, the best -- probably the best way, because there is an audio-tape on this, that the verification request is given to the Registry and the interpreters, and then they re-tape the -- they put the tape on and then the -- this provisional -- this actually part is re-interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that would -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, to interrupt you. I think this is probably the easiest way and the most -- the less complicated way than anything else. Because if we -- in this case if we go into repeating the question, the answer, there might be -- there might be -- first of all, the time will be lost. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure. The only thing that you have to do is to identify those parts in the transcript of today --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honour, I know how to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and ask to have it verified. And this is said without any criticism to our interpreters, with whom I have great confidence in them. You're always very good. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may on this point, Your Honour, I would request -- if there are particularly concerning or important ones, that they be expedited as quickly as possible. Because if it turns out that the correct translation is something dramatically different from what I understood it to be, then I would need the opportunity to try and address it with the witness before he leaves town. That's my only concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Gentlemen, we are being advised by the Registry that the process of formal verification takes a longer time than the witness -- this witness is expected to stay in town. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that that is typically how it works. I guess I'm just trying to raise the issue that if it is a particularly important matter, that perhaps with CLSS or the appropriate parties it could be expedited if there's only, you know, five lines at page 73, it seems to me as a practical matter it wouldn't take that long for one person to listen and verify. I understand if we're making a request for the entire transcript or several pages, that's different. But if there is one particular item, like the last answer, if with the Court's assistance we could perhaps urge CLSS to make an exception to the ordinary process. That's my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What we'll do is we'll have a word with CLSS in the next break and then see how things can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I can ask for nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, sorry for the interruption. Let me go next then to page 33 in your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in e-court 33 in the English, 34 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the top we have three names, the chief of the Doboj centre who you told us about before, the chief of the Doboj SJB, and the deputy for the Doboj CSB, Milan Savic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what do you know about him, what prior experience did he have in the police before the conflict began in 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Savic worked in the crime technicians' department of the public security centre. He had completed some kind of secondary or high school and completed a course in pyrotechnics. When I was in Doboj in July and later in August, until the end of that year I visited a couple of times. There was one occasion when his colleague, who also worked in the crime technicians' department, his name was Novica - I can't remember his last name - had a private trading company in Doboj, and he was retired but as a reserve worker. He worked in the Doboj public security centre during the war. They said, "Well, let's go and drink coffee right across the street from the public security centre at his shop," it was in the main street. So we did. This was after August 1992. Now, why am I saying this? Because in August 1992, together with a colleague, Nikola Milanovic, I had an assignment from the minister's cabinet to make a review of the events in Teslic, to look at that file. It was a very voluminous file, and we needed to take an overview and complete a report so that the minister would be totally informed about what really happened there. We did that. I don't need to go into re-telling of that event now. So on that occasion when we were drinking coffee I said, "You were in Teslic there the chief of those guys in Doboj, and you were creating a lot of problems?" So then he understood that I knew a lot about that particular case, and then in order to make an impression on me - that's at least how I understood it - that he was an important person as the deputy of the chief of the Doboj centre, Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic, not educated, with just secondary school, he was telling me, he was boasting, "Do you know what I did in 1991 in order to get to where I am now, to this post?" I didn't want to ask him about that and that's not my habit. I usually let a person speak by themselves, and he was open to me. Novica was there and his wife was there who was a Bosniak. She was sitting at the cash register and taking money from people who were buying some things. We were just sitting very close to there, and he then said to me, "I was in a group which the Doboj SDS at the time formed in order to blow up buildings such as the political parties' newly formed in 1990 in the Doboj region." And he told me in detail the story of how they went to Odzak - this is a place in north-Eastern Bosnia on the left bank of the Bosna River. It's a small town of some 15.000, mainly Bosniak and Catholic population. They arrived there at about 1900 hours, and they placed an explosive device, a plastic explosive device. Very simply they stuck a fuse on it, and it was a time-activated fuse. From Odzak to Modrica they were driving there. It was 6 kilometres, so they were rushing to the evening news to some local cafe to hear the news, whether this happened or not. Did it blow up. And how they were happy about that. I think that he did tell me the truth there --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Just to clarify, who was telling you this, the name of the individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Milan Savic, this was Milan Savic. And this was the reason why he advanced in the service, because he had had a role in certain actions of the SDS with a group of people. He didn't mention any names. I didn't question that because it was war, and if you ask him that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then when he continued the story --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The interpreter indicated that she didn't hear what you said after you said: "I didn't question that because it was war, and if you ask him that ..." they were not able to catch what you said after that. Can you carry on from that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to ask him, "Who were you with? Give me some names or mention somebody," that would be suspicious to them. And since he knew where I was from, where I was coming from, naturally he didn't want to open up the topic any more. I used the term "zakuje" meaning block up. He actually wanted to let me know by that act that as far as he was concerned I was not an important person during those three days that I was in Doboj. I was just a small figure and that he was the one who could take the credit for the fact that the Serbian rule was now in force in Doboj, even though the structure of the population was 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. When you were in Doboj in the middle of August, 15th of August, Milan Savic was -- was still the deputy of the CSB, of the regional security centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not there by then because of that event in Teslic. He was arrested with a group of operative who had committed some abuses in Teslic. I don't know how long they were in detention. Criminal report was submitted by the Banja Luka security centre. So I really couldn't say when he was released with the others who had been detained. After that I think that he was no longer a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The event in Teslic, you're talking about from notorious events involving a group that was referred to as the Mice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware of whether or not Milan Savic was ever charged with any crime in connection with the activities of the Mice; and if so, whether he was ever convicted or removed from the MUP because of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Savic was not convicted because of that in the sense of war crimes, but he was convicted pursuant to the criminal report by the Banja Luka security services centre. This is an unfortunate incident -- or when two -- well, when members of the same police draw weapons -- actually, my personal position regarding that particular case is that Mr. Zupljanin, either alone or with somebody else's approval, decided to stop the abuses of those people that they were committing in Teslic, expulsions, seizure of property, terror acts. This went on for two months that they were terrorising those people, and this was -- a stop was put to this in June when Andrija Bjelosevic, Milan Savic were arrested, who was going with him with 75.000 German marks in his pocket, and Andrija doesn't know where this money had come from, with weapons and other things perhaps. Colleagues that had directly participated in the work on that case will have something more to say about that. But just by looking at the case, the overview, that's how I was able to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said that Milan Savic was convicted pursuant to a criminal report by the Banja Luka security services centre. Do you know any details about that? When and where was he convicted and for what? Was it any kind of crime against non-Serbs, or was it for crimes against other Serbs, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a criminal report was submitted, but I don't know what the outcome was really. I didn't really follow-up to see what had happened. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit 1439 -- 65 ter 1439, that's the notes from the diary that we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P403 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honour, I'd like to go into private session for the next few documents if I may. We break at 10.25?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to show you 65 ter 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand -- actually this already has an exhibit number of 1D59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What about 65 ter 304?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I meant to tender that under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted as Exhibit 405 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This exhibit, 1D59, in evidence, have you seen this document before or during 1992 were you aware of the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this document because such documents are usually sent to the chiefs of organisational units and administrations, and it is up to them to proceed in a responsible and conscientious manner to take action upon such documents. I was just a person who executed orders. I heard about it but I was not really involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any circumstances in 1992 where members of the MUP who were criminally prosecuted or against whom criminal proceedings were being conducted were dismissed from duty and placed at the disposal of the army, of the VRS? Did you know about that happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of certain cases through violations committed, for instance, people who were trying to help their family members, Bosniaks or Catholics. I know of several such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were -- I'm sorry. Were those persons -- were those persons actually criminally prosecute, or were they merely removed from the service and turned over to the army, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were disciplined. There were disciplinary proceedings held within the Ministry of the Interior. There was a disciplinary commission, and at the proposal of the chief of an organisational unit, proceedings, disciplinary proceedings, would be held from the station level and to higher levels up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct in understanding that not everyone who was disciplined internally was dismissed and/or turned over to the army, talking about MUP personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were examples where people were not held responsible, either in disciplinary or criminal proceedings for all sorts of reasons. For instance, if I may mention the case of the Samac group. This is Stevan Todorovic who was chief of the public security station without a formal decision on appointment, you know what he was tried for and you know what crimes he had committed. He stayed on until 1994 in that position. Now, who kept them there, I don't know. But I know that the minister did not appoint him; the politicians appointed him, Mr. Blagaj Simic did and Mr. Radovan Karadzic also, he was close to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you now another document. This is 65 ter 239. And I will tell you, sir, this is a 9 September 1992 meeting on Mount Jahorina of the extended board of the RS MUP. And I'm not -- I know you weren't at the meeting. I'm not asking you about that. I want to ask you about something that will be found at page 6 of the English and for you beginning at the bottom of page 3 in the B/C/S which will be on the screen in a moment. And at the meeting one of the things that was discussed was personnel issues. At the bottom of your page number 1 listed is Dragan Andan and it says he was: " ... temporarily suspended for illegal use of poker machines ..." Do you know what happened to Mr. Andan after that temporary suspension? He remained in the service, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber allows me, I would take a while to explain exactly what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm hoping -- I'll certainly defer to whatever the Judges want to do, but I would ask you now if you could just answer my question. Did Mr. Andan remain in the service in 1992 after his temporary suspension?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was thrown out of the service and he joined the Army of Republika Srpska. This was a glaring example of violation of discipline by employees of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He returned to the service at a later time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much later. I was retired in 2000 and sometime after that - I don't know using what connections - he returned and became director of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go to the next page in B/C/S in e-court. We can stay on the same page in English. I have one more to ask you about, Witness. Number 2 on the list is: "Danilo Vukovic, temporarily suspended for unbecoming behaviour and reckless endangerment." First of all, did you know who he was and where he worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my first senior in wartime. He used to work in the former republic SUP in Sarajevo as inspector of white-collar crime, because he's an economist by training. Somebody sent him to Bijeljina to become chief of the sector of crime police in Bijeljina, just before the Bijeljina centre was set up. On one occasion he occupied some Bosniak apartment down-town, on the fourth or fifth floor. He lived there alone, and with a friend of his he spent all the time somewhere down-town. And then later in his apartment he would continue drinking, and when he was completely drunk he took a bomb, defensive or offensive, I don't know, and threw it from the apartment from the fifth floor to the side of the street where people keep their cars. And there are many passers-by. It was in the summer, in July I think. This grenade exploded and put the lives of people below at risk. A complete on-site investigation was conducted, and the whole case was differed to the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. Whether he was later prosecuted, I don't know, but I know that after that incident he was excluded from the service, again by a decision of the minister's office because this is really a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if he was turned over to the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not turned over to the army because he managed to avoid it. He had a decision on him, a decision on appointment. He went to join his family in Montenegro and stayed in hiding there until the charges were too old to be prosecuted. His wife was a native of Bosanska Gradiska, so he later returned there. He kept a low profile for a while, but eventually he committed another criminal act involving a fire-arm. And he was charged for that after the war. Still, he was again admitted to the Ministry of the Interior by a decision of Dragan Kijac, then minister, because the two of them had a kum, best man, relationship. So those are the type of unlawful acts I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we now go into private session before I show the witness the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were being issued your ID, including those rights and powers that authorised officials have - and the rights are stated on the back of your ID card - when you were issued with that ID card and your service pistol, did you maybe sign such a solemn statement, declaration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not preferred to us. I just signed for my official ID in the personnel section, and I also drew from supplies a service pistol, handcuffs, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you don't remember signing such a solemn declaration in the personnel service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that that was a practice in the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't remember any of my colleagues making such a solemn declaration -- at least I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry, we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- is from the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, signed by Minister Mico Stanisic. The date is 19 July 1992, sent to all security services centre, to the attention of the chief, and the document resulted from the conclusions endorsed at the first meeting of the collegium of the MUP on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade. In paragraph 1 it says: "... among priority tasks for the national security service and the crime prevention service, the tasks on detecting and documenting war crimes ..." And then there is a reference to another order of the 16th of May, 1992 -- so the -- "discovery and documentation of war crimes, of genocide, and the submission of criminal reports were among the priorities of the national security service and crime prevention service, a questionnaire on war crimes and victims of genocide has been compiled in the information analysis administration." Can we now show page 3 and the form of this questionnaire. I'd like to ask you for two comments. You see points 5 and 6: "Ethnicity and religion" of the victim of war crime. When you were making this questionnaire with your senior officers and colleagues with whom you investigated the war crimes and Yellow Wasps, did you fill a similar questionnaire with similar information that was security related?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this questionnaire much later, when it was already well in use after many of our interventions and reviews. But in the days in which it was developed, I did not see it. I've already said how exactly I took the statement and made an official note concerning Dusan Vuckovic, a.k.a. Repic. This was mostly used by the State Security Service, and our jurisdictions were different. But of course if I found something out, I could always write an official note - nobody would stop me - and make it available to the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "State Security Service," between the Public Security Service to which you belonged and the State Security Service, the jobs were divided concerning the documentation of war crimes and the primary organ responsible for this was the State Security Service. Could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think they were mainly responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But at any rate, if I understood your evidence correctly, even you - although you were in the Public Security Service - were involved as part of the team investigating the Yellow Wasps for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not forbidden from getting involved, on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "on the contrary," that means you received orders to join that team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not with a clear conscience keep something like that to myself when I was talking to the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you started these inspections in the summer of 1992, were there any complaints concerning the possibilities of communication between public security stations and security services centres or internally within them, were such complaints in April through July 1992, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April until July I was not aware of that, but by 15 July communications were working between what was then the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska and what was the Federation today. There were also working telephone lines. You could call Bijeljina, Prijedor, Trebinje from Banja Luka and other places. As for other communications, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's go back to that interview of the 15th of August, that talk. That's when you first heard about this Teslic problem; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. After that meeting and after a report was written to inform the leadership about the situation in the police, the crime incidents, and the level of equipment available to the police, only later did we receive instructions from Minister Stanisic to go to the Banja Luka centre - it was already August - to look into that case, make an analysis, make a report, and inform the ministry exhaustively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In fact, it was at that meeting that you first learned in detail about the problems that existed between the CSB Doboj and the SJB Doboj, that is, the centre and the police station, and further into the territory Samac, Derventa, and Teslic. It was put to you for the first time as a problem and you received for the first time an explanation of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it was the priority issue at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were explaining -- we don't have much time so I am not going to open up that new aspect. Let me just ask you: Today when you were talking about the Teslic problem, when the political leadership decided that Teslic should belong to the Banja Luka region, and thereby also change the jurisdiction of the security services centre over a certain public security station, my learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you about the situation in Zvornik. And you went on to explain that before the war, in 1992, Zvornik belonged to the security services centre Tuzla, where you used to work. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the CSB also included Bijeljina as well as Zvornik at that time. Before the war there was no CSB in Bijeljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't there before. It was formed in June 1992 for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Tuzla CSB wasn't in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it was in the Federation territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that the public security station in Zvornik was practically -- when Republika Srpska was established and until the CSB was formed, remained without its original centre, the CSB which was in Tuzla at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But this was then compensated for quickly with the forming of the Bijeljina CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I think that it is now clear, the situation. Do you remember that Mr. Bjelosevic, the chief of the CSB, complained about the relationship or the attitude of Bijeljina CSB towards the Prijedor SJB [as interpreted], is that correct, but more specifically in relation to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-121 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were more complaints from the army headed by Commander Slavko Lisica. I think he wrote quite voluminous documents to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will come to that. What I'm interested in now is the Crisis Staff. I wanted to show you a document before we finish for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness 1D700.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You are aware that he complained about the problems that he was having with the Crisis Staff, do you recall that? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, can I ask my learned friend if the transcript is correct at page 83, lines 22 and 23. The Bijeljina CSB towards the Prijedor SJB?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It has nothing to do with Prijedor. The Crisis Staff -- the Crisis Staff of Doboj, not Prijedor CJB. I said the Crisis Staff of Doboj. The problems which the chief of CSB had with the Crisis Staff of Doboj. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please look at this document, sir. I don't know whether you were ever shown it before. It's the decision of the Crisis Staff in Doboj dated the 15th of June, 1992. It's a couple of decisions at a meeting held on the 15th of May, and it adopted certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because it's time for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. I will probably take a minute -- a couple of minutes, so I guess we can leave it for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I apologise. We will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Witness, I remind you of what I would have said yesterday, that you can't discuss your testimony until you -- well, you -- while you're still sworn as a witness. So we resume until -- and re-convene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
